content: Glyburide is a hypoglycemic agent approved by the FDA for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus. Common adverse reactions include epigastric fullness, heartburn, and nausea. When transitioning patients from glyburide (micronized) tablets or other oral hypoglycemic agents, retitration is necessary. There is no fixed dosage regimen for managing diabetes mellitus with glyburide or other hypoglycemic agents. Blood glucose levels must be monitored periodically, in addition to urinary glucose, to determine the minimum effective dose, detect primary failure (inadequate glucose lowering at maximum recommended dose), and identify secondary failure (loss of adequate glucose control after initial effectiveness). Glycosylated hemoglobin levels may also be valuable in monitoring therapeutic response. Short-term administration of glyburide may suffice during periods of transient loss of control in patients usually well-controlled on diet alone. The usual starting dose of glyburide tablets is 2.5 to 5 mg daily, administered with breakfast or the first main meal. Patients more sensitive to hypoglycemic drugs should start at 1.25 mg daily. Failure to adhere to an appropriate dosage regimen may precipitate hypoglycemia. Patients who do not follow their prescribed dietary and drug regimen are more likely to exhibit unsatisfactory therapeutic responses. When transferring patients from other oral antidiabetic therapies to glyburide, the process should be conservative, with an initial daily dose of 2.5 to 5 mg. No transition period or priming dose is necessary when switching from oral hypoglycemic agents other than chlorpropamide. However, when transferring from chlorpropamide, particular care is required during the first two weeks due to prolonged retention of chlorpropamide in the body and overlapping drug effects, which may provoke hypoglycemia. Some type 2 diabetic patients treated with insulin may respond satisfactorily to glyburide. If the insulin dose is less than 20 units daily, substitution with glyburide tablets (2.5 to 5 mg as a single daily dose) may be attempted. For insulin doses between 20 and 40 units daily, patients may be placed directly on glyburide tablets (5 mg daily as a single dose). For insulin doses exceeding 40 units daily, a transition period is required, during which insulin dosage is reduced by 50% and glyburide tablets (5 mg daily) are initiated. Progressive withdrawal of insulin and incremental increases in glyburide dosage (1.25 to 2.5 mg every 2 to 10 days) are then carried out. During this conversion period, hypoglycemia may rarely occur. Patients should test their urine for glucose and acetone at least three times daily and report results to their physician. Persistent acetonuria with glycosuria indicates the need for insulin therapy in type 1 diabetes. Therefore, glyburide tablets should be administered at least 4 hours prior to colesevelam. The usual maintenance dose of glyburide ranges from 1.25 to 20 mg daily, given as a single dose or in divided doses. Dosage increases should not exceed 2.5 mg at weekly intervals, based on blood glucose response. No exact dosage relationship exists between glyburide and other oral hypoglycemic agents. Patients transferred from the maximum dose of other sulfonylureas should not exceed a starting dose of 5 mg of glyburide. A maintenance dose of 5 mg of glyburide provides similar blood glucose control as 250 to 375 mg of chlorpropamide, 250 to 375 mg of tolazamide, 500 to 750 mg of acetohexamide, or 1000 to 1500 mg of tolbutamide. Daily doses exceeding 20 mg are not recommended. Once-daily therapy is usually sufficient, but some patients, particularly those on more than 10 mg daily, may respond better to twice-daily dosing. Glyburide is contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to the drug, diabetic ketoacidosis (with or without coma), type 1 diabetes mellitus, and concomitant administration of bosentan. Oral hypoglycemic drugs, including glyburide, have been associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular mortality compared to treatment with diet alone or diet plus insulin. This warning is based on findings from the University Group Diabetes Program (UGDP) study, which reported a 2.5-fold increase in cardiovascular mortality in patients treated with tolbutamide compared to those on diet alone. All sulfonylureas, including glyburide, can cause severe hypoglycemia. Proper patient selection, dosage, and instructions are critical to avoid hypoglycemic episodes. Renal or hepatic insufficiency may elevate glyburide levels and diminish gluconeogenic capacity, increasing the risk of serious hypoglycemic reactions. Elderly, debilitated, or malnourished patients, and those with adrenal or pituitary insufficiency, are particularly susceptible to hypoglycemia. Hypoglycemia may be difficult to recognize in the elderly and in patients taking beta-adrenergic blocking drugs. It is more likely to occur with deficient caloric intake, severe or prolonged exercise, alcohol ingestion, or the use of multiple glucose-lowering drugs. Loss of blood glucose control may occur during stress, such as fever, trauma, infection, or surgery, necessitating discontinuation of glyburide and initiation of insulin therapy. The effectiveness of glyburide in lowering blood glucose may decrease over time due to disease progression or diminished drug responsiveness, a phenomenon known as secondary failure. Treatment of patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency with sulfonylureas, including glyburide, can lead to hemolytic anemia. A non-sulfonylurea alternative should be considered for these patients. Hemolytic anemia has also been reported in patients without known G6PD deficiency. Therapeutic response to glyburide should be monitored with frequent urine glucose tests and periodic blood glucose tests. Adverse reactions include hypoglycemia, cholestatic jaundice, hepatitis, and rare progression to liver failure. Gastrointestinal disturbances such as nausea, epigastric fullness, and heartburn are common and dose-related. Allergic skin reactions, including pruritus, erythema, urticaria, and maculopapular eruptions, have been reported. Hematologic reactions, including leukopenia, agranulocytosis, thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, aplastic anemia, and pancytopenia, have been reported. Metabolic reactions, such as hepatic porphyria and disulfiram-like reactions, are rare. Cases of hyponatremia and syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) have been reported. Glyburide is classified as pregnancy category B by the FDA. Animal studies have shown no evidence of harm to the fetus, but there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Prolonged severe hypoglycemia has been reported in neonates born to mothers receiving sulfonylureas at the time of delivery. Glyburide should be discontinued at least two weeks before the expected delivery date. Safety and effectiveness in pediatric patients have not been established. Elderly patients are particularly susceptible to hypoglycemia, and conservative dosing is recommended to avoid adverse reactions.
